title: Why the Iran Deal Will Hold
gist: Video page from Foreign Policy editor Ravi Agrawal arguing the U.S.-Iran deal will hold; the captured text contains no transcript, only the headline and surrounding FP coverage that flags skepticism about Trump's follow-through and ambiguity over the Strait of Hormuz.

insights.claim: Foreign Policy editor in chief Ravi Agrawal argues, in a June 2026 video segment, that the U.S.-Iran peace deal will hold.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: A durable deal lowers the probability of renewed Gulf conflict and oil-supply disruption risk premia.
insights.locator: Why the Iran Deal Will Hold

insights.claim: Foreign Policy's companion coverage questions the U.S.-Iran deal's durability, arguing that, as the Gaza agreement showed, Trump is better at fanfare than follow-up.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Weak implementation risk means headline deals may not translate into lasting de-escalation; keep geopolitical hedges.
insights.quote: As his Gaza agreement has shown, Trump is better at fanfare than follow-up.
insights.locator: How the Iran Deal Sets the Stage for More Conflict

insights.claim: Foreign Policy coverage flags that the U.S.-Iran deal is hazy on the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the status of the key oil chokepoint unclear.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Unresolved Hormuz terms keep tail risk in shipping, tanker rates and crude prices alive despite a deal.
insights.quote: The Iran Deal Is Hazy on Hormuz

insights.claim: Foreign Policy coverage argues ordinary Iranians will not see any of the money flowing from Trump's Iran deal.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: If economic benefits do not reach the population, domestic instability in Iran could undermine the deal over time.
insights.quote: Ordinary Iranians Won’t See a Dime of Trump’s Money
